questions.question: Compare Spring bean scopes (singleton, prototype, request, session, application) and when to use each.
questions.title: Spring Bean Scopes: Singleton, Prototype, Request, Session, Application
questions.direct_answer: Spring's default is **singleton** — one instance per container, cached and reused. **Prototype** creates a new instance every time it's requested; useful for stateful helpers but Spring does *not* destroy them (you manage lifecycle). **Request**, **session**, and **application** scopes (web only) tie a bean's lifetime to an HTTP request, session, or `ServletContext`. **`@RefreshScope`** (Spring Cloud) re-creates the bean when config changes. **Common pitfalls**: injecting a prototype bean into a singleton freezes it to one instance (use `ObjectProvider<T>`, `@Lookup`, or scoped proxy); stateful singletons cause race conditions; request-scoped beans require an active HTTP request. **Default**: keep beans singleton and stateless; use prototype rarely; avoid session-scope for horizontally scaled apps unless sticky sessions or a shared session store are in place.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of scope trade-offs, prototype injection into singleton pitfall, stateless design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating singletons as stateful; naive @Autowired of prototype; session-scope in scaled-out apps
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss ObjectProvider, @Lookup, scoped proxy modes, @RefreshScope, thread-safety implications

sections.title: What Bean Scope Means
Scope Lifetimes — How Long Each Bean Lives
sections.content:
The diagram below maps the four most common scopes to their lifetime windows. Notice that **singleton spans the entire application**, **prototype is gone the moment you stop holding it**, and **request/session live only as long as their HTTP artifact**. ```mermaid flowchart LR Start(["Application start"]) Sing["Singleton bean
created once at startup
lives until shutdown"] Stop(["Application shutdown"]) ReqA(["HTTP request A starts"]) ReqAEnd(["HTTP request A ends"]) ReqAR["Request-scoped bean A
created on first use
destroyed at request end"] ProtoA["Prototype bean #1
new for call site A"] ProtoB["Prototype bean #2
new for call site B"] ReqB(["HTTP request B starts"]) ReqBEnd(["HTTP request B ends"]) ReqBR["Request-scoped bean B
different instance from A"] Sess(["Session created"]) SessEnd(["Session expires"]) SessB["Session-scoped bean
shared across all
requests in session"] Start --> Sing --> Stop ReqA --> ReqAR --> ReqAEnd ReqA --> ProtoA ReqA --> ProtoB ReqB --> ReqBR --> ReqBEnd Sess --> SessB --> SessEnd ReqA -.belongs to.-> Sess ReqB -.belongs to.-> Sess ``` **Reading the diagram** - Singleton is created at startup and outlives every request - Prototype instances appear at the call site and Spring forgets about them immediately after construction - Request-scoped beans are different instances per request; the session-scoped bean is shared across requests within the same session

sections.title: Scopes Compared
sections.content:
The table below maps each scope to its lifetime, thread-safety burden, and the situation it exists to solve.

| Scope | Instances | Lifetime | Thread-safety requirement | Web required | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **singleton** | 1 per context | Context lifetime | Yes; beans usually stateless | No | Services, repos, config |
| **prototype** | New per request | Until GC; container doesn't destroy | Caller's problem | No | Stateful workers, one-shot helpers |
| **request** | 1 per HTTP request | End of request | Per request (usually single thread) | Yes | Request metadata, per-request cache |
| **session** | 1 per HTTP session | Session timeout | Multi-tab issues | Yes | User preferences, wizard state |
| **application** | 1 per ServletContext | Application lifetime | Yes | Yes | Similar to singleton for web context |
| **websocket** | 1 per WS session | WS session | Yes | Yes | WS-specific state |
| **`@RefreshScope`** | Replaced on refresh | Until next refresh event | Yes | No | Cloud Config live reload |

sections.title: Prototype Injection into Singleton — The Classic Pitfall
Best Practices and When to Use Each
sections.content:
**`singleton` (default) — used for ~99% of beans**
- Services, repositories, controllers, factories, utilities
- **Must be thread-safe**: keep them stateless; any state must be local to method or synchronized
- `@ConfigurationProperties` objects are singletons
- Heavy objects (caches, clients with connection pools) — singleton amortizes cost

**`prototype` — rare, but valid for**
- Stateful workers that should not be shared across requests
- One-shot helpers whose state matters (builder patterns)
- Legacy code that mutates beans
- **Spring does not call `@PreDestroy` on prototypes** — manage lifecycle yourself

**`request` — per-request state**
- Request tracing / correlation IDs (though MDC is simpler)
- Per-request caches (only within one request)
- Always use `proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS` when injecting into singletons

**`session` — use sparingly**
- Wizard / multi-step form state
- Short-term user preferences in session
- **Avoid in horizontally scaled apps** without sticky sessions or shared session store (Spring Session + Redis)
- Consider: is session state better stored client-side or in explicit DB?

**`application` / `websocket` — niche web-context scopes**

**`@RefreshScope` (Spring Cloud)**
- Beans whose behavior depends on external config
- `/actuator/refresh` triggers recreation
- Useful for changing feature flags, log levels, rate limits at runtime

**Common pitfalls**
- **Stateful singleton** — the #1 source of concurrency bugs
- **Injecting prototype naively** — gets one instance forever
- **Forgetting `proxyMode`** on web scopes injected into singletons
- **Session scope in scaled-out apps** without sticky sessions or Spring Session
- **Long-lived prototype beans** — no lifecycle management means leaks
- **Custom scopes without registration** — must register with `CustomScopeConfigurer`

sections.title: Trade-offs and Real-World Patterns
sections.content:
**When singleton helps:**
- Stateless services scale horizontally with zero overhead
- Heavy resources (connection pools, caches) construct once and amortize
- DI graph wired at startup; no runtime reflection cost
- Pushes you toward stateless design — the right default for scalability

**When prototype helps:**
- Genuine per-use mutable state (builder objects, batch processors with internal counters)
- Avoids accidental sharing of mutable state across threads
- When method-local `new` would lose Spring features (AOP, injection)

**When request/session scope helps:**
- Per-request caches that dedupe work within one HTTP cycle
- Multi-step wizards where state must persist across requests in one session
- Audit / tracing where carrying state through method params is awkward

**When it hurts:**
- Stateful singleton — race conditions, lost updates, the #1 production bug
- Prototype injected without `ObjectProvider` — silently behaves like singleton
- Session scope in horizontally scaled apps — pod death loses state, breaks load balancing
- `@RefreshScope` overuse — references in non-refreshable beans go stale

**Watch for:**
- `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor` (default for `@Async`) creates unbounded threads — prefer bounded `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor`
- Mixing scopes in the dependency graph requires correct proxy mode or `ObjectProvider`
- Session state forces sticky sessions on the load balancer; consider Spring Session + Redis or moving state to a token

**Custom scopes — when justified**
- Multi-tenant beans (one instance per tenant, evicted when tenant context clears)
- Feature-flag-scoped beans (different bean per flag value)
- Implement `Scope`, register with `CustomScopeConfigurer`, then `@Scope("tenant")`

**Strategic take**
- Default to singleton + stateless; that solves 95% of designs
- Extract per-request state to DTOs or MDC rather than request-scoped beans
- Avoid session scope unless you've thought about horizontal scaling
- Use `ObjectProvider<T>` when you need a fresh non-singleton instance

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Singleton** (default) — one per context; must be stateless / thread-safe; covers ~99% of beans.
- **Prototype** — fresh instance per request; Spring doesn't manage lifecycle after construction; no `@PreDestroy` callback.
- **Request / session / application** — web-only; lifetime tied to HTTP artifacts.
- **Injecting prototype/request into singleton** — use `ObjectProvider<T>`, `@Lookup`, or scoped proxy.
- **`ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS`** — CGLIB proxy; `INTERFACES` — JDK proxy.
- **`@RefreshScope`** — bean recreated on Spring Cloud config refresh; useful for live-reloadable feature flags.
- **Custom scopes** via `Scope` + `CustomScopeConfigurer` — tenant-scoped, feature-flag-scoped beans.
- **Pitfalls** — stateful singletons (concurrency bugs), prototype injection freezing, session scope breaking horizontal scale.
- **Default stance** — singletons + stateless; prototype rarely; session-scope only with sticky sessions or shared store.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring's default is singleton — one instance per container, shared everywhere. Prototype creates a new instance every request. Request, session, and application scopes are web-only and tie the bean's lifetime to HTTP artifacts.

**Spring Core scopes**
- singleton — one per `ApplicationContext`, shared
- prototype — new instance every request; Spring stops managing it after construction

**Web-aware scopes**
- request — one per HTTP request
- session — one per HTTP session
- application — one per `ServletContext`
- websocket — one per WebSocket session

**Additional**
- `@RefreshScope` (Spring Cloud) — recreated on `/actuator/refresh`

**The classic pitfall — prototype injected into singleton**
- `@Autowired` runs once at bean construction; the singleton gets one prototype instance forever
- Fix with `ObjectProvider<T>` (recommended), `@Lookup`, or scoped proxy with `proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS`
- Same fix needed for request/session-scoped beans injected into singletons

**Best practice by scope**
- singleton — 99% of beans, must be stateless and thread-safe
- prototype — rare; only when per-use mutable state is genuine; remember Spring won't run `@PreDestroy`
- request — per-request caches and tracing; MDC often simpler
- session — wizards and preferences; avoid in horizontally scaled apps without Spring Session + Redis or sticky sessions

**Strategic take**
- Default to stateless singletons — that's what makes Spring apps scale horizontally
- Fighting that default usually means you're storing state in the wrong place

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean?
questions.title: @Component vs @Bean — Two Ways to Register Beans
questions.direct_answer: **`@Component`** is a **class-level** annotation discovered by **component scanning** — Spring instantiates the class and manages it as a bean. **`@Bean`** is a **method-level** annotation inside `@Configuration` classes — you write the construction logic explicitly and return the instance Spring should manage. Use `@Component` for classes you own and want to mark as Spring-managed. Use `@Bean` for **third-party classes you don't control** (you can't add `@Component` to `RestTemplate`), for **conditional or parameterized construction**, and when you need **multiple beans of the same type** with different configs. `@Component` is convention-based; `@Bean` is explicit and gives full control over instantiation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that @Component and @Bean serve different scenarios — class ownership vs explicit factory method — and when to reach for each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying they're interchangeable, or trying to put @Component on a third-party class (you can't modify a class you don't own).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @Bean methods inside @Configuration classes are CGLIB-proxied so calling one method from another returns the same bean, and that this proxying doesn't apply to @Component classes.

sections.title: Two Registration Mechanisms — One Implicit, One Explicit
sections.content:
**`@Component` and `@Bean` both register beans** with the Spring container, but they target different scenarios.

**`@Component` is implicit registration via component scanning**.
- You annotate a class you own with `@Component` (or one of its specializations: `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`).
- When component scan reaches that package, Spring instantiates the class using its constructor and registers the resulting object as a bean.
- The framework picks the constructor and manages everything.

**`@Bean` is explicit registration via factory method**.
- You write a method inside a `@Configuration` class, annotate it with `@Bean`, and return the object you want Spring to manage.
- You control everything: which constructor, what arguments, conditional logic, post-construction setup.
- The method name becomes the bean ID by default.

**The fundamental decision**: do you own the class? If yes and the construction is straightforward, `@Component`. If no (third-party library), or yes but construction needs logic, `@Bean`.

sections.title: @Component vs @Bean — Side-by-Side
sections.content:
Each row maps a real characteristic to how the two annotations behave.

| Aspect | `@Component` | `@Bean` |
|---|---|---|
| **Where applied** | Class declaration | Method inside `@Configuration` class |
| **Discovery** | Component scanning of packages | Explicit method invocation by Spring |
| **Who calls the constructor** | Spring (using its own DI logic) | You, in the method body |
| **Class ownership** | Must be your class (need to add annotation) | Works for any class, including third-party |
| **Construction logic** | Limited to constructor injection | Arbitrary logic — conditionals, builders, factory calls |
| **Multiple instances of same type** | Awkward (need different classes or qualifiers) | Easy — multiple `@Bean` methods returning same type |
| **Inter-bean references** | Via `@Autowired` | Method calls (CGLIB-proxied for singleton semantics) |
| **Bean name default** | Class name camelCased | Method name |
| **Conditional registration** | `@ConditionalOnX` on the class | `@ConditionalOnX` on the method (more flexible) |
| **Test override** | Hard — need to exclude from scan | Easy — override the `@Bean` method in a test config |

**The most operationally important row** is *class ownership*. You can't put `@Component` on `RestTemplate` because you don't own its source. That's the most common reason to reach for `@Bean`.

sections.title: When to Use @Component
When to Use @Bean
Common Pitfalls and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**Putting `@Bean` outside a `@Configuration` class**
- `@Bean` works in `@Component`-annotated classes too, but **without CGLIB proxying**
- Inter-bean method calls then create new instances each time — silent singleton breakage
- Always put `@Bean` methods inside `@Configuration` classes unless you specifically don't need inter-method singleton semantics

**Trying to put `@Component` on a third-party class**
- You'd need to subclass it just to add the annotation — defeats the point
- Use `@Bean` instead

**Bean name collision**
- Two `@Bean` methods in different `@Configuration` classes returning the same type with the same method name will conflict
- `@Component` collisions happen when two classes have the same simple name in different packages
- Resolve with explicit `name` attribute or `@Qualifier`

**Conditional registration**
- `@ConditionalOnX` annotations work on both `@Bean` methods and `@Component` classes
- More common on `@Bean` methods because conditional logic for third-party integration usually belongs in configuration

**Test override**
- `@Bean` is much easier to override in tests — just declare a `@TestConfiguration` with the same method name and return type
- `@Component` requires excluding from component scan, which is more involved

**The factory method bridge**
- For complex object graphs, `@Bean` methods can call helper static methods or builders
- This separates the configuration concern from the domain logic

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Component` is class-level, scanned**; **`@Bean` is method-level, explicit** — they target different scenarios.
- **Use `@Component` for your own classes** with straightforward construction — services, repositories, controllers.
- **Use `@Bean` for third-party classes** — `RestTemplate`, `DataSource`, `ObjectMapper` — you can't add annotations to them.
- **Use `@Bean` for multiple instances of same type** — two `DataSource` beans with different configs, distinguished by `@Primary` and `@Qualifier`.
- **`@Configuration` classes are CGLIB-proxied** — calling one `@Bean` method from another returns the same singleton; this doesn't apply to `@Component` classes.
- **`@Bean` is easier to override in tests** — `@TestConfiguration` with same method name; `@Component` requires excluding from scan.
- **Conditional registration works on both** — `@ConditionalOnX` on `@Bean` method or `@Component` class; more flexible on `@Bean`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Both `@Component` and `@Bean` register objects with the Spring container, but they solve different problems.

**`@Component` — class-level, scanned**
- Annotate a class you own; component scan instantiates it and registers it as a bean
- Specializations: `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`
- Best for your own services, repositories, controllers — straightforward construction

**`@Bean` — method-level, explicit**
- Inside a `@Configuration` class, write a method that returns the object Spring should manage
- You control everything: constructor choice, arguments, conditional logic
- Best for third-party classes you don't own (`RestTemplate`, `DataSource`), parameterized construction, and when you need multiple beans of the same type

**The decision rule**
- Do you own the class? If yes and construction is straightforward, `@Component`
- If no, or if construction needs logic, `@Bean`

**Subtle but important — CGLIB proxying**
- `@Configuration` classes are subclassed by CGLIB at runtime
- Calling one `@Bean` method from another inside the config class returns the same singleton instance — Spring intercepts the call
- This doesn't happen with `@Component`-annotated classes — inter-method calls construct fresh instances
- Always put `@Bean` methods inside `@Configuration`, not `@Component`

**Other practical advantages of `@Bean`**
- Easy to override in tests (`@TestConfiguration` with same method name)
- Easy to register multiple instances of same type with `@Primary` and `@Qualifier`
- Conditional registration via `@ConditionalOnX` on the method

questions.question: What is the difference between @Autowired, @Inject, and @Resource?
questions.title: @Autowired vs @Inject vs @Resource — Three Injection Annotations
questions.direct_answer: All three perform **dependency injection** but come from different specifications and use different resolution strategies. **`@Autowired`** (Spring) injects **by type** by default; falls back to name with `@Qualifier`. **`@Inject`** (JSR-330) is the **standard Java DI annotation** — same by-type resolution as `@Autowired` but with no `required=false` option (use `Optional<T>` or `Provider<T>`). **`@Resource`** (JSR-250 / Jakarta) injects **by name first**, then by type — the opposite of `@Autowired`. Use `@Autowired` for Spring-only projects, `@Inject` for portable code that might run on other DI containers, and `@Resource` only when you specifically want name-first resolution (typically for legacy Java EE code).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows these three annotations exist, understands the type-vs-name resolution difference, and can explain when each is the right choice.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying they're identical, or not knowing that @Resource resolves by name first while @Autowired resolves by type first.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that constructor injection is recommended over field injection for testability, that @Inject + Provider<T> is the JSR-330 equivalent of ObjectProvider, and that @Resource on the field name is what makes it ambiguity-friendly.

sections.title: Three Annotations, Three Resolution Strategies
sections.content:
**Spring supports three dependency injection annotations** — each from a different specification and with different resolution semantics.

**`@Autowired`** is **Spring-native** (`org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation`).
- It resolves dependencies **by type** first; if multiple beans of that type exist, it falls back to matching the field name as a bean name, or you use `@Qualifier` to disambiguate.
- It supports `required = false` for optional dependencies.

**`@Inject`** is the **JSR-330 standard** (`jakarta.inject.Inject` / `javax.inject.Inject`).
- It works the same way as `@Autowired` for type-based resolution but is **not Spring-specific** — code using `@Inject` can run on Guice, CDI, Dagger, or any JSR-330-compliant container.
- It has no `required` flag; use `Optional<T>` or `Provider<T>` for optional or lazy dependencies.

**`@Resource`** is **JSR-250 / Jakarta Annotations** (`jakarta.annotation.Resource`). It resolves **by name first**, falling back to type — the opposite of `@Autowired`. Originally designed for Java EE resource injection (`DataSource`, `EJB`), Spring honors it for parity with the spec.

**The decision rule**: `@Autowired` for Spring-only code, `@Inject` for portability, `@Resource` for name-first resolution or legacy Java EE compatibility.

sections.title: @Autowired vs @Inject vs @Resource
sections.content:
Each row maps a real concern to how each annotation handles it.

| Aspect | `@Autowired` | `@Inject` | `@Resource` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Specification** | Spring | JSR-330 (standard Java DI) | JSR-250 / Jakarta Annotations |
| **Package** | `org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation` | `jakarta.inject` | `jakarta.annotation` |
| **Resolution order** | By type first, then by name | By type first, then by `@Named` qualifier | By name first, then by type |
| **Optional dependency** | `required = false` | Wrap in `Optional<T>` or `Provider<T>` | `lookup` attribute or wrap in `Optional<T>` |
| **Disambiguation** | `@Qualifier("name")` | `@Named("name")` | `name` attribute on `@Resource` |
| **Portability** | Spring-only | Any JSR-330 container (Spring, Guice, CDI) | Java EE / Jakarta EE compatible |
| **Constructor injection** | Yes (recommended) | Yes (recommended) | No (field/setter only) |
| **Static field injection** | No | No | No |

**The most operationally important row** is *resolution order*. `@Autowired` and `@Inject` agree (type first); `@Resource` is the contrarian (name first). This single fact determines which one to use when multiple beans of the same type exist.

sections.title: @Autowired — Spring's Native Choice
@Inject — The Portable Standard
@Resource — Name-First Resolution
sections.content:
**`@Resource` is JSR-250 / Jakarta Annotations** — originally designed for Java EE resource injection but recognized by Spring.

**The defining feature: by name first**
- `@Resource` looks up the bean **by name** before considering type
- Uses the `name` attribute, then falls back to the field name as the bean name
- Only if no name match, falls back to type-based resolution

**Example — explicit name**

```java
@Resource(name = "primaryDataSource")
private DataSource dataSource;
```

- Looks for a bean named `primaryDataSource` regardless of type matches

**Example — implicit name (field name)**

```java
@Resource
private DataSource readonlyDataSource;
```

- Looks for a bean named `readonlyDataSource`
- Matches the field name to the bean name
- Convenient when bean names align with field names

**When `@Resource` makes sense**
- Multiple beans of the same type where name-based selection is more readable than `@Qualifier`
- Legacy Java EE code being migrated to Spring (preserves existing semantics)
- Strict adherence to Jakarta EE conventions

**Limitations**
- **No constructor injection** — only field and setter
- Less popular in modern Spring code; `@Autowired` + `@Qualifier` covers most cases
- Field injection is harder to test

**Why some teams prefer `@Resource` for `DataSource`-style beans**
- When you have multiple `DataSource` beans (`primary`, `readonly`, `audit`), naming the field exactly the bean name eliminates the need for separate `@Qualifier` annotations
- The field name itself documents the dependency

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Autowired` is Spring-native** — resolves **by type**, then falls back to field name; supports `required = false`.
- **`@Inject` is JSR-330 standard** — same type-first resolution; portable across Spring, Guice, CDI, Dagger; no `required` flag (use `Optional<T>` or `Provider<T>`).
- **`@Resource` is JSR-250** — resolves **by name first**, then by type; opposite of `@Autowired`; field/setter only, no constructor injection.
- **`@Qualifier` (Spring) and `@Named` (JSR-330) disambiguate** when multiple beans of the same type exist.
- **Constructor injection is preferred** for `@Autowired` and `@Inject` — enables `final` fields and easier testing.
- **Spring 4.3+ makes `@Autowired` optional on a single constructor** — Spring auto-detects and injects.
- **`@Resource` shines for name-based DataSource selection** — field name matches bean name, no separate qualifier needed.
- **Avoid mixing `@Autowired` and `@Inject` in the same class** — pick one per project for consistency.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
All three annotations perform dependency injection, but they come from different specifications and resolve dependencies differently.

**`@Autowired` — Spring-native**
- Resolves by type first; falls back to bean name matching the field name
- Use `@Qualifier("name")` to disambiguate when multiple beans of the same type exist
- Supports `required = false` for optional dependencies
- Constructor injection is preferred — enables `final` fields and easier testing
- Since Spring 4.3, optional on a single constructor — Spring auto-detects

**`@Inject` — JSR-330 standard**
- Same type-first resolution as `@Autowired`
- Portable: works on Spring, Guice, CDI, Dagger — any JSR-330 container
- Disambiguation via `@Named("name")` instead of `@Qualifier`
- No `required` flag — use `Optional<T>` for optional, `Provider<T>` for lazy/per-call
- Best for shared library code or hexagonal architecture

**`@Resource` — JSR-250 / Jakarta**
- Resolves by name first, then by type — opposite of `@Autowired`
- Field/setter only — no constructor injection
- Useful for legacy Java EE code or when name-based DataSource selection is more readable than `@Qualifier`
- Field name matches bean name implicitly — convenient pattern

**The decision rule**
- Spring-only project: `@Autowired`
- Portable library code: `@Inject`
- Name-first resolution or Java EE migration: `@Resource`

Most modern Spring codebases standardize on `@Autowired` with constructor injection — that's the idiomatic choice.

questions.question: What is the difference between ApplicationContext and BeanFactory?
questions.title: ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory — Two Container Interfaces
questions.direct_answer: **`BeanFactory`** is the **root container interface** — provides basic bean lookup and lifecycle management. It's lazy: beans are created **on first access**. **`ApplicationContext`** is a **superset of `BeanFactory`** — adds enterprise features: **eager singleton initialization at startup**, **event publishing** (`ApplicationEventPublisher`), **internationalization** (`MessageSource`), **resource loading** (`ResourceLoader`), **environment abstraction**, and **automatic `BeanPostProcessor` and `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` registration**. In modern Spring applications, you almost always use `ApplicationContext` (or its specializations like `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext`). `BeanFactory` is now mostly a **legacy interface** retained for backward compatibility and resource-constrained environments where eager initialization is undesirable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory and adds enterprise features, and knows about eager vs lazy initialization differences.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying they're unrelated, or not knowing ApplicationContext is a superset of BeanFactory with significant additional capabilities.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that ApplicationContext eagerly initializes singletons at startup (fail-fast), automatically detects and registers BeanPostProcessor/BeanFactoryPostProcessor instances, and publishes ContextRefreshedEvent.

sections.title: Two Interfaces, One Inheritance
sections.content:
**`BeanFactory` is the root interface** of Spring's IoC container.
- Provides the absolute minimum: register bean definitions, look up beans by name or type, manage their lifecycle.
- **Lazy by design** — beans are instantiated only when first requested via `getBean()`.

**`ApplicationContext` extends `BeanFactory`** and layers on enterprise features:
- Eagerly initializes all singleton beans at startup — fail-fast on misconfiguration.
- Automatically registers `BeanPostProcessor` and `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` instances.
- Publishes lifecycle events (`ContextRefreshedEvent`, `ContextClosedEvent`).
- Supports internationalization via `MessageSource`.
- Loads resources from classpath / file / URL via `ResourceLoader`.
- Provides environment abstraction — `Environment`, profiles, property sources.

**The practical reality**: in 99% of Spring applications you use `ApplicationContext` — typically `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` or Spring Boot's `AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext`.
- `BeanFactory` is mostly a **legacy abstraction** retained for backward compatibility.
- Reach for it directly only in resource-constrained scenarios (Android, embedded systems) where lazy initialization matters, or when writing custom container infrastructure.

sections.title: Inheritance and Capability — How ApplicationContext Builds on BeanFactory
sections.content:
The diagram shows the interface hierarchy and what each level adds. `ApplicationContext` is `BeanFactory` plus six enterprise capabilities. ```mermaid flowchart TB BF["BeanFactory

sections.title: ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory — Feature Matrix
sections.content:
Each row maps a capability to whether it's available in each interface.

| Feature | `BeanFactory` | `ApplicationContext` |
|---|---|---|
| **Bean lookup (`getBean()`)** | Yes | Yes (inherited) |
| **Lazy initialization** | Yes (default) | Optional (eager by default) |
| **Eager singleton init at startup** | No | Yes (fail-fast) |
| **Automatic `BeanPostProcessor` registration** | No (manual) | Yes |
| **Automatic `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` registration** | No (manual) | Yes |
| **Event publishing (`ApplicationEventPublisher`)** | No | Yes |
| **Internationalization (`MessageSource`)** | No | Yes |
| **Resource loading (`ResourceLoader`)** | No | Yes (classpath, file, URL) |
| **Environment abstraction (`Environment`)** | No | Yes (profiles, property sources) |
| **AOP support (`@AspectJ` autoproxy)** | No (manual setup) | Yes (auto via post-processor) |
| **Common implementation** | `XmlBeanFactory` (deprecated) | `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext`, `ClassPathXmlApplicationContext` |

**The critical row** is *eager singleton init at startup*. `BeanFactory` waits until you call `getBean()` to construct a bean — silent failures hide until first use. `ApplicationContext` constructs every singleton at startup, surfacing misconfiguration immediately. This is why production Spring apps overwhelmingly use `ApplicationContext`.

sections.title: Eager vs Lazy Initialization — The Defining Behavioral Difference
sections.content:
**`BeanFactory` is lazy by default**
- Beans are constructed only when first requested via `getBean()`
- Misconfiguration (wrong constructor args, missing dependencies) doesn't surface until that bean is actually used
- A typo in a `@Value` injection might survive deployment and only fail at runtime when the bean is needed

**`ApplicationContext` is eager by default for singletons**
- Every singleton bean is constructed at startup (during `refresh()`)
- Misconfiguration fails fast — the application doesn't start, so you find errors before serving traffic
- This is the **fail-fast principle** in action

**Why eager is the right default for production**
- Errors found at startup, not in production traffic
- Health checks accurately reflect application readiness
- Connection pools, caches, and singletons that have construction cost amortize before the first request

**When lazy initialization is still useful**
- Heavy beans only some deployments use (e.g., a feature-flagged integration)
- Annotate individual beans with `@Lazy` to defer construction
- Spring Boot 2.2+ supports `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` to make all beans lazy globally — useful for fast development restarts but not recommended for production

**Example — lazy on a specific bean**

```java
@Bean
@Lazy
public ExpensiveReportingService reportingService() {
    return new ExpensiveReportingService();
}
```

- Bean constructed only when first injected/requested
- Other beans that depend on it get a proxy until needed

sections.title: Other Enterprise Features ApplicationContext Adds
sections.content:
**Automatic `BeanPostProcessor` registration**
- `BeanPostProcessor` instances are how Spring AOP, `@Autowired` injection, and many extensions work
- `BeanFactory` doesn't auto-detect them — you must register manually with `addBeanPostProcessor()`
- `ApplicationContext` automatically detects every `BeanPostProcessor` bean and applies it to all subsequent bean creations
- Same for `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` (operates on bean definitions before instantiation)

**Event publishing (`ApplicationEventPublisher`)**
- `ApplicationContext` implements `ApplicationEventPublisher`
- `publishEvent(event)` notifies all `@EventListener`-annotated methods and `ApplicationListener` beans
- `BeanFactory` has no event support — Spring Events don't work without `ApplicationContext`

**Internationalization (`MessageSource`)**
- `ApplicationContext` exposes `getMessage(code, args, locale)` for resolving locale-specific messages
- Backed by `ResourceBundleMessageSource` or `ReloadableResourceBundleMessageSource`
- `BeanFactory` has no concept of i18n

**Resource loading (`ResourceLoader`)**
- `ApplicationContext` is a `ResourceLoader` — `getResource("classpath:config.properties")` returns a `Resource`
- Supports `classpath:`, `file:`, `http:` prefixes
- Used internally by `@PropertySource`, `@ImportResource`

**Environment abstraction (`Environment`)**
- Profiles: `getActiveProfiles()`, `getDefaultProfiles()`
- Property sources: `getProperty("key")` reads from `application.properties`, env vars, system properties
- Foundation for `@Profile`, `@ConfigurationProperties`, `@Value` resolution

**Lifecycle events**
- `ContextRefreshedEvent` fires when context is initialized
- `ContextClosedEvent` fires before shutdown
- `BeanFactory` has no lifecycle event mechanism

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`ApplicationContext` extends `BeanFactory`** — superset relationship; not a competitor.
- **`BeanFactory` is lazy** — beans constructed on first `getBean()`; misconfiguration surfaces at runtime.
- **`ApplicationContext` is eager for singletons** — all singletons constructed at startup; fail-fast on misconfiguration.
- **Auto-registration of post-processors** — `ApplicationContext` detects `BeanPostProcessor` and `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` automatically; `BeanFactory` requires manual registration.
- **Event publishing only in `ApplicationContext`** — `ApplicationEventPublisher`, `@EventListener`, lifecycle events all require `ApplicationContext`.
- **Resource loading and i18n** — `ResourceLoader`, `MessageSource`, `Environment` are `ApplicationContext` features.
- **Use `@Lazy` on individual beans** to defer construction even within `ApplicationContext`.
- **`BeanFactory` is largely legacy** — almost every modern Spring app uses `ApplicationContext` (via `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` or Spring Boot's web variant).
- **`spring.main.lazy-initialization=true`** (Spring Boot 2.2+) — global lazy init for fast dev restarts; not recommended for production.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`ApplicationContext` extends `BeanFactory`. They're not alternatives — they're a superset/subset relationship. The difference is what each adds beyond basic bean lookup.

**`BeanFactory` — the root container**
- Provides basic bean lookup, registration, and lifecycle
- Lazy by default — beans constructed on first `getBean()`
- No event publishing, no i18n, no resource loading, no environment abstraction
- Mostly legacy now — retained for backward compatibility and resource-constrained scenarios

**`ApplicationContext` — the enterprise container**
- Superset of `BeanFactory`
- Eager singleton init at startup — fail-fast on misconfiguration
- Auto-registers `BeanPostProcessor` and `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` (this is how AOP, `@Autowired`, and most extensions work)
- Event publishing via `ApplicationEventPublisher` and `@EventListener`
- Internationalization via `MessageSource`
- Resource loading via `ResourceLoader` (`classpath:`, `file:`, `http:`)
- Environment abstraction with profiles and property sources
- Lifecycle events: `ContextRefreshedEvent`, `ContextClosedEvent`

**The defining behavioral difference**
- `BeanFactory` lazy initialization — misconfiguration hides until first use
- `ApplicationContext` eager singleton init — misconfiguration surfaces at startup, fail-fast
- This is why production Spring apps overwhelmingly use `ApplicationContext`

**Practical guidance**
- In modern Spring, you almost always use `ApplicationContext` — typically `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` or, in Spring Boot, `AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext`
- Use `@Lazy` on individual beans if you need to defer construction
- `BeanFactory` is for the rare resource-constrained scenario; production apps use `ApplicationContext`
